growth_story.headline: Chile's income per person grew 5.7 percent a year in 1990–1997, 3.1 through 2013 and 1.1 since, as the copper boom faded and productivity stalled.
growth_story.arc: After a decade of market reforms, Chile's income per person grew 5.7 percent a year in 1990–1997, the fastest of its three eras since 1990. The Asian crisis hurt Chile's terms of trade and export volumes, income per person fell 1.5 percent in 1999, and growth then settled at 3.1 percent a year through 2013. From 2014 the pace dropped to 1.1 percent a year: investment weakened as the copper price outlook dimmed, and the World Bank traces the longer slide mainly to weak productivity growth, in mining and beyond. The pandemic cut income per person by 7.0 percent in 2020 before a 10.8 percent rebound in 2021, but growth had already been slow for six years before it. Income per person grew 2.0 percent in 2025 and reached its highest level yet, though mining disruptions pulled the economy back in the first half of 2026.

threads.title: A decade of reforms
threads.text: Income per person grew 5.7 percent a year in 1990–1997. An IMF article from 2000 credited the reforms of that decade for the record, and the IMF noted in 2025 that growth has not come close to that pace since.

threads.title: The Asian crisis shock
threads.text: The Asian crisis hurt Chile's terms of trade and the volume of its exports. Income per person fell 1.5 percent in 1999, a short dip before growth resumed.

threads.title: The copper boom fades
threads.text: Growth in income per person fell from 2.3 percent in 2013 to 0.8 percent in 2014, the start of the slow era. The IMF tied the slowdown in part to a weaker copper price outlook that held back investment.

citations.title: Press Release: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2014 Article IV Consultation with Chile
citations.quote: Investment has weakened and growth slowed markedly in part due to a weaker copper price outlook.

threads.title: Productivity stalls, demography drags
threads.text: The World Bank traces the long slowdown mainly to weak productivity growth, linked to falling copper ore grades but also spread across the rest of the economy, and describes two decades of it. The IMF adds that demographic change alone trims the pace the economy can sustain.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Chile (October 2026)
citations.quote: The main driver is weak total factor productivity growth, rooted in declining copper ore grades but also widespread in the non-mining sector.

citations.title: Chile Can Grow Faster – But it Won’t Be Like the 1990s Again

threads.title: Mining setbacks, new government
threads.text: Mining output shrank in the second half of 2025 and fell again in the first half of 2026, as ore grades declined and maintenance disrupted work. A new government took office in March 2026 with a focus on fiscal discipline, more efficient regulation and drawing investment.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Chile (October 2026)

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 2.0 percent in 2025 and reached its highest level yet. Then the economy shrank in the first half of 2026, as mining was disrupted, the job market softened and higher oil prices pushed up inflation.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Chile (October 2026)
citations.quote: The economy contracted 0.3 percent in the first half of 2026, weighed down by mining disruptions, a softening labor market, and rising inflationary pressures.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Chile (October 2026)
citations.quote: Inflation climbed to 4.3 percent, driven by rising international oil prices, impacting on real wages and moderating private consumption.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes two decades of weak productivity, a span that starts around 2006. Yet income per person grew 2.9 percent a year in 2006–2015, and the sharp break in the data comes only in 2014. For years, weak productivity and solid growth ran side by side.
